newsitem.title: USA: Peru Bradys extend gains as hostage crisis ends.
newsitem.headline: Peru Bradys extend gains as hostage crisis ends.

text.p: Peruvian Brady bonds rose sharply on Tuesday, outperforming the broader emerging debt market, after troops stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima and local television said all but one of the 72 hostages had been rescued alive.

"It looks as though we are up again. There may a little more upward movement but not much more from where we are now. It's probably a little bit overbought but then we are up quite substantially," said Richard Segal, head of emerging market fixed income at Santander Investment.
Though Peruvian Bradys scored sharp gains after the rescue mission, some emerging market debt experts said the bonds may have limited upside potential given the steep price gains on Tuesday.

"I think the market is a little bit overbought because this was not as much a drag on the market as this rally would suggest, and I think that the overall market conditions will weigh more heavily on Peru," said Walter Molano, head of economic and financial research at SBC Warburg in New York.

"Peru is going to be very susceptible to the movement in U.S. rates, so I think Peru will continue experiencing what the other instruments of the other countries have been experiencing, and that is a tendency towards a decline in prices," Molano added.
Still, the initial reaction was one of exuberance.
At 1830 EDT/2330 GMT, Peru PDI bonds were 7/8 higher at 58-1/4 and the country's FLIRBs were 1-3/4 better at 53-1/4 bid.

Market sources said the rescue operation essentially removed a major liability for Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori and would allow market participants to focus much more closely on the economic fundamentals.
"Maybe now, we can analyze the macroeconomic situation more closely and that is quite good," said another source.
In the broader emerging debt market, traders said a powerful rally by U.S. blue chip stocks and a strong advance by the Treasury bond market helped to push prices higher.
The Dow Jones industrial average surged 173 points to close at 6834, and the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury climbed 18/32 to end at 94.26, producing a yield of 7.04 percent.

In other news that contributed to the positive tone, Standard and Poor's Corp said it revised a policy that would essentially allow certain issuers in so-called dollarized economies -- where currencies are closely pegged to the U.S. dollar -- to enjoy a higher rating than the sovereign ceiling.
Argentina was one of the countries affected by the rating action, and market sources said price gains reflected the news.
"It sure has affected the market. Argentina is trading higher as are the Argentine corporates," said one Brady bond trader at a U.S. investment firm.

In its report, S&P said the foreign currency ratings it assigned to private sector borrowers in Latin countries with dollarized economies would more fully reflect their stand-alone credit characteristics.
Argentine Global 17 bonds surged 1-3/8 to 104-3/8 and its FRBs rose 5/8 to 90-5/8.
